# Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct

## Our Pledge

We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, caste, color, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.

We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

## Our Standards

Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our community include:

* Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people
* Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
* Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
* Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes, and learning from the experience
* Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall community

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

* The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances of any kind
* Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
* Public or private harassment
* Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or email address, without their explicit permission
* Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

## Enforcement Responsibilities

Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for moderation decisions when appropriate.

## Scope

This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces. Examples of representing our community include using an official e-mail address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.

## Enforcement

Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported to the community leaders responsible for enforcement at [me@gorkemkaryol.dev](mailto:me@gorkemkaryol.dev). All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly.

All community leaders are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the reporter of any incident.

## Enforcement Guidelines

Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

### 1. Correction

**Community Impact**: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.

**Consequence**: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the behavior was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.

### 2. Warning

**Community Impact**: A violation through a single incident or series of actions.

**Consequence**: A warning with consequences for continued behavior. No interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.

### 3. Temporary Ban

**Community Impact**: A serious violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior.

**Consequence**: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period. Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.

### 4. Permanent Ban

**Community Impact**: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.

**Consequence**: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within the community.

## Attribution

This Code of Conduct is adapted from the [Contributor Covenant][homepage], version 2.1, available at [https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct.html][v2.1].

Community Impact Guidelines were inspired by [Mozilla's code of conduct enforcement ladder][Mozilla CoC].

For answers to common questions about this code of conduct, see the FAQ at [https://www.contributor-covenant.org/faq][FAQ]. Translations are available at [https://www.contributor-covenant.org/translations][translations].

[homepage]: https://www.contributor-covenant.org

`CONTRIBUTING.md`:

```md
# Contributing to rigcheck

Thanks for helping! rigcheck is a small project, so the most useful contributions are often small too: a wrong verdict reported with details, a translation fix, or a capture of your hardware.

By taking part you agree to the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Security problems go through [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md), not public issues.

## Quick ways to help

### Report a wrong verdict

Open a [Wrong verdict](https://github.com/Glory42/rigcheck/issues/new?template=wrong-verdict.yml) issue with the game, the stamp you got, what you expected, and the text from **My Rig → Copy as text**. If you know the game runs (or doesn't), say how well and with which Proton version.

### Fix hardware the app doesn't recognize

Verdicts need to know your CPU and GPU. Both live in [`data/hardware.toml`](data/hardware.toml):

- **A name isn't matched** (the game page shows Steam's text but no comparison): add an `aliases` entry to the right part.
- **A part is missing**: add it with a rough `score` (GPUs relative to a GTX 1060 6GB = 100, CPUs relative to an i5-4460 = 100) and, for GPUs, its PCI ID if you know it. The tests in `crates/core/tests/catalog.rs` show how names are matched.

### Share your machine as a test fixture

Hardware detection is tested against captured machines in [`data/fixtures/hardware/`](data/fixtures/hardware/). Five of the six are hand-written; real captures are better:

```sh
data/fixtures/hardware/capture.sh my-machine-name
```

It copies only the files detection reads (`/proc/cpuinfo`, `/proc/meminfo`, `/sys/class/drm/*`, `/etc/os-release`, and `vulkaninfo` / `nvidia-smi` output). Look through the folder before you commit it, then open a PR. The [fixtures README](data/fixtures/hardware/README.md) has the details.

### Translate

UI text lives in [`app/i18n/`](app/i18n/) as [Fluent](https://projectfluent.org) files: `en.ftl`, `tr.ftl`, `de.ftl`.

- To fix a translation, edit the line in that language's file.
- To add a language, copy `en.ftl`, translate every line, and add the language to `Language` in [`app/src/i18n.rs`](app/src/i18n.rs).
- Write uppercase labels in uppercase yourself (`AYARLAR`, `EINSTELLUNGEN`). The code never uppercases text, because that gets letters like Turkish İ wrong.

A test fails if any language is missing a line, so `cargo test` tells you when you're done.

## Development

Setup and everyday commands are in the [README](README.md#development). Before opening a PR, run what CI runs:

```sh
cargo fmt --all
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test --workspace
cargo deny check bans
```

The UI tests render offscreen. On a machine without a GPU, set `ICED_TEST_BACKEND=tiny-skia`, as CI does.

### How code gets written here

- **Test first.** Write a failing test, then just enough code to pass it, one behavior at a time. A test that passes on its first run should be shown to fail when the code is broken.
- **Test through public interfaces.** Tests call a crate's public functions (or click through the UI with `iced_test`), not private helpers, so code can be refactored without rewriting tests.
- **Expected values come from outside the code**: Steam's text, a worked example, the roadmap. Not from running the code and copying its output.
- **Real data over invented data.** Fixtures are captured from real machines and real store pages where possible.
- **Keep `crates/core` pure** (no files, no network). Only `crates/net` may use an HTTP client; `cargo deny check bans` enforces it.

The [roadmap](ROADMAP.md) says what's planned and why. For anything bigger than a fix, open an issue first so we can agree on the approach.

### Pull requests

- Branch from `master` and keep each PR to one topic.
- Write commit messages that say what changed and why.
- The [PR template](.github/pull_request_template.md) asks for a summary (a diagram, call tree or file tree beats prose), evidence (a test that failed before and passes now, or a screenshot), and how risky the merge is.

## License

Code contributions are MIT licensed, like the rest of the code ([LICENSE](LICENSE)). Data contributions to `data/` are included in the published game database, which will be licensed under the ODbL (see [ROADMAP §1.2](ROADMAP.md#12-licenses)).

```

`README.md`:

```md
<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/brand/icon-128.png" alt="" width="112">
</p>

<h1 align="center">rigcheck</h1>

<p align="center">
  <b>Can my PC run it?</b><br>
  A Linux desktop app that checks your Steam games against your hardware, and against Linux itself.
</p>

<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/screenshots/library.webp" alt="The Library: installed Steam games as cover tiles with READY, TOO WEAK and BLOCKED stamps" width="820">
</p>

> [!NOTE]
> **Pre-1.0 (v0.7).** Everything below works today. The game database is rebuilt daily from Steam; its store pages are read a few thousand a day, so most of Steam's ~200k games are known by name only for now, and get looked up live when you open them. See the [roadmap](ROADMAP.md).

## What it does

- **Reads your Steam library.** It finds native, `~/.steam` and Flatpak installs and every library folder, including other drives, and skips Proton and the Steam runtimes.
- **Detects your hardware.** It reads CPU, RAM, every GPU by its PCI ID, video memory, the Vulkan version and the driver straight from `/proc`, `/sys` and `vulkaninfo`. Hybrid laptops use the discrete GPU, and it warns if your NVIDIA card runs on `nouveau`.
- **Gives every game a verdict.** It compares your PC with the game's minimum and recommended specs, names the part holding you back, and takes Linux into account: ProtonDB ratings, anti-cheat that blocks Linux, and the Vulkan version Proton needs.
- **Searches all of Steam.** The Catalog lists every game, most popular first, and filters it: only games your PC can run, ProtonDB tier, native Linux, Deck Verified, no anti-cheat problems. A game the database hasn't checked yet is looked up on Steam when you open it.
- **Lets you ask "what if?"** Pick a different GPU or CPU on My Rig and every verdict updates.
- **Keeps itself current.** The game database updates in the background, and the app tells you when a new version is out.

| Stamp | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `READY` | Meets the recommended specs |
| `LOW` | Meets the minimum; at least one part falls short of recommended |
| `TOO WEAK` | At least one part is below the minimum, and the game page says which |
| `BLOCKED` | Can't run on Linux whatever the hardware, e.g. anti-cheat that denies Linux |
| `???` | Not enough data to say |

<sub>Screenshots from the real app on the real game database, rendered offscreen with its test renderer on a Ryzen 5 7530U laptop with Radeon integrated graphics (`app/src/screenshots.rs`).</sub>

## Privacy

Local-first: no accounts, no telemetry, no servers of our own. Nothing about you or your PC leaves your machine.

The app sends plain, read-only requests to three places, and nowhere else ([ROADMAP §6](ROADMAP.md#6-privacy--network)):

| Where | When | What's sent |
|---|---|---|
| `github.com` (Releases) | At start: is there a newer game database, or a newer rigcheck? Downloads the database when there is | Nothing but the file request |
| `store.steampowered.com` | When you open a game the database hasn't checked yet | That game's app ID |
| `shared.akamai.steamstatic.com` | Cover art Steam hasn't cached on your disk | The game's app ID |

Settings → Privacy turns the start-up checks off (then they run only when you ask), and lists the same three places. A build rule (`deny.toml`) keeps HTTP clients out of every crate except `crates/net`, which refuses any other host.

## Install

Each [release](https://github.com/Glory42/rigcheck/releases) has an **AppImage** (any distro), a **.deb** (Debian, Ubuntu, Mint), an **.rpm** (Fedora, openSUSE) and a tarball. An AUR package (`rigcheck-bin`) and a Flathub listing are on the way; their recipes are in [`packaging/`](packaging/).

Install `vulkan-tools` as well, so rigcheck can read your GPU's Vulkan version and video memory.

## Build from source

Arch is shown; any distro with `rustup` works. No GUI packages are needed to build, since iced loads Wayland, X11 and Vulkan at runtime.

```sh
sudo pacman -S --needed rustup base-devel
rustup default stable            # includes clippy and rustfmt
git clone https://github.com/Glory42/rigcheck && cd rigcheck
cargo run -p rigcheck --release
```

## Development

All Rust: a Cargo workspace with the desktop app (built with [iced](https://iced.rs)), the data pipeline and shared crates. The code is built test-first.

```
app/          desktop app: Library, Catalog, game page, My Rig, Settings, About (binary: rigcheck)
  i18n/       translations (Fluent): en, tr, de
crates/
  core/       requirement parser, hardware table matching, matcher (no I/O)
  hardware/   Linux hardware detection
  steam/      Steam installs, libraries and cover art
  gamedb/     games.db and fetched.db (SQLite): schema, queries, verdicts, safe install
  net/        the only crate allowed an HTTP client; refuses hosts off its allowlist
pipeline/     data pipeline that builds games.db daily (GitHub Actions)
packaging/    desktop file, AppStream metainfo, AppImage/deb/rpm, AUR and Flatpak recipes
data/         hardware table, seed games, test fixtures
```

```sh
cargo install cargo-deny --locked
cargo test --workspace           # all tests; UI tests run headless
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --all
cargo deny check bans            # only crates/net may use an HTTP client
INSTA_UPDATE=always cargo test -p rigcheck-core --test parser   # accept parser snapshot changes, then review the diff
```

CI runs fmt, clippy, tests and `cargo deny` on pushes to `master` and on pull requests. Screenshots are rendered by an ignored test: `RIGCHECK_SCREENSHOT_DB=<a games.db> cargo test -p rigcheck screenshots -- --ignored`.

## Contributing

Wrong verdicts, missing hardware, translations and captures of your machine all help. [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) explains each, plus how code gets written here (test-first). Please follow the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md), and report security problems privately as described in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

## Credits

- Game data comes from Steam's store pages; Proton compatibility from [ProtonDB](https://www.protondb.com) reports ([ODbL](https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/odbl/1-0/)), rated by rigcheck's own rule ([ROADMAP §9](ROADMAP.md#9-data-sources--licenses)); anti-cheat status from [AreWeAntiCheatYet](https://areweanticheatyet.com) (MIT); Steam Deck status from Steam's Deck compatibility reports.
- Requirement text in `data/fixtures/requirements/` comes from Steam's store pages, for testing the parser.
- Hardware scores in `data/hardware.toml` are rough hand estimates. The published database fills in parts the table lacks from [Blender Open Data](https://opendata.blender.org) (CC0), and GPU PCI IDs come from [pci.ids](https://pci-ids.ucw.cz).
- The pixel-art icon is original, drawn by scripts in [`assets/brand/`](assets/brand/).

## License

`ROADMAP.md`:

```md
# ROADMAP

> **Working name:** `rigcheck` (placeholder, rename freely)
>
> A Linux desktop app that tells you whether your PC can run a game before you buy it. It checks your installed Steam library and can search every game on Steam. Beyond raw hardware, it covers the Linux-specific questions: Proton compatibility, anti-cheat, drivers and Vulkan.

---

## 1. Principles

These are the rules every decision below follows. If a feature breaks one of them, the feature changes, not the principle.

1. **Local-first.** All game data, hardware info and results live on the user's machine. The app works offline once the database is downloaded.
2. **Zero user data.** No accounts, no telemetry, no analytics, no crash reporting servers. The app never sends the user's hardware, library or searches anywhere.
3. **No servers.** The project hosts no database and no API. The only thing published is a static database file, on GitHub Releases.
4. **Zero cost.** Everything runs on free tiers: a public GitHub repo, GitHub Actions, GitHub Releases, Flathub and AUR.
5. **Honest results.** If the app can't parse a requirement or identify a piece of hardware, it says **"unknown"** and shows the raw text. It never invents confidence.
6. **Open source (MIT).** The code is MIT-licensed. The repo stays **private during early development** and goes public before the data pipeline starts publishing (see §1.1). Being public gives free GitHub Actions and public release downloads, satisfies the data licenses (see §9) and earns trust from Linux users.

### 1.1 Repository visibility plan

| Stage | Visibility | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Phases 0–3 | **Private** | Early, messy work. CI runs fit in the free private quota (2,000 Actions minutes/month on GitHub Free) |
| Before Phase 4 | **Public** | Required for zero cost: release assets in a private repo need authentication, so the app couldn't download `games.db` or app updates. A daily crawl would also use up the private Actions quota within days |

**While private:**
- Run CI only on pushes to `master` and on pull requests.
- Cache Rust builds (`Swatinem/rust-cache`) to save minutes.
- Develop against the hand-written seed database instead of a published one.

**Before going public:** check that no secrets are in the git history, and make sure the README, LICENSE and credits are in place.

### 1.2 Licenses

| What | License |
|---|---|
| Code (app, crates, pipeline) | **MIT** |
| Published `games.db` | **ODbL**: required because it includes ProtonDB data, which is ODbL (share-alike) |

### Non-goals
- No Windows/macOS support. Linux only.
- No user-submitted reports or community database. ProtonDB already does this, and it would need a server and user data.
- No FPS predictions. Results are "meets minimum / recommended", not "62 fps on High".
- No game stores other than Steam in v1. GOG and Epic come later, if ever (see §11).

---

## 2. What the app does

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| **My Library** | Lists every installed Steam game with cover art and a verdict badge (✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ / ❓) |
| **Catalog** | Instant search across every game on Steam, owned or not |
| **Game page** | Per-component verdict (CPU, GPU, RAM, VRAM, storage, graphics API), the bottleneck component, ProtonDB rating, anti-cheat status, Steam Deck status and a native Linux flag |
| **My Hardware** | Shows detected CPU, GPU(s), RAM, VRAM, driver, Vulkan version, distro, kernel and free disk space |
| **Appearance** | Five color themes for the pixel-art look (Paper, Ink, Midnight, Plum, Forest). Paper is the default; the choice is saved in `settings.json` |
| **Language** | English, Turkish and German (Fluent `.ftl` files in `app/i18n/`). Follows the system language unless the user picks one. Game names and Steam's requirement text stay in English |
| **Storage settings** | Database size and update status, a clear button for the cache, an image cache limit |

### Verdict levels
| Badge | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ✅ **Recommended** | Every component meets the recommended specs |
| 🟢 **Minimum** | Every component meets the minimum specs, at least one falls short of recommended |
| ❌ **Below minimum** | At least one component is below minimum. The app names it |
| ⛔ **Blocked** | The game can't run on Linux regardless of hardware, e.g. anti-cheat that denies Linux or a ProtonDB "Borked" rating |
| ❓ **Unknown** | Not enough data. The app shows the raw requirement text |

The overall verdict is the **worst component**. A ⛔ Linux blocker overrides every hardware verdict.

---

## 3. Architecture

```
┌──────────────────── Desktop app (one Rust binary, iced) ───────────────┐
│                                                                        │
│  app/  UI: Library │ Catalog │ Game page │ My Hardware │ Settings      │
│        Elm architecture: state → view → Message → update               │
│        calls the crates below directly (no IPC, no webview)            │
│  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
│  crates/                                                               │
│  ├── hardware   detect CPU/GPU/RAM/VRAM/Vulkan/driver/disk             │
│  ├── steam      find Steam installs, list installed games              │
│  ├── gamedb     games.db (read-only) + fetched.db (cache), updater     │
│  ├── net        the ONLY crate with an HTTP client: live Steam         │
│  │              lookups, cover art download, games.db download         │
│  └── core       requirement parser + matcher (shared with pipeline)    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          │ only 3 network destinations, all read-only, all via net (§6)
          ▼
   GitHub Releases (games.db)   Steam store API (live lookups)   Steam CDN (images)

┌──────────────────── Data pipeline (GitHub Actions, scheduled) ─────────┐
│ 1. Download the previous games.db release                              │
│ 2. Fetch Steam app list → find new/changed games                       │
│ 3. Crawl requirements (rate-limited, resumable)                        │
│ 4. Parse with `core` → structured requirements                         │
│ 5. Join ProtonDB dump, AreWeAntiCheatYet, hardware scores              │
│ 6. Validate → compress → publish games.db + manifest.json              │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Key idea:** the requirement parser and matcher live in a single Rust crate (`core`). The pipeline uses it to pre-parse popular games, and the app uses the **same code** to parse live-fetched games. One parser, one source of truth.

---

## 4. Tech stack

| Layer | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Language | **Rust, everywhere** | One language for UI, logic and pipeline. A single native binary, no webview |
| UI | **iced** (0.14) | Native Rust GUI in the Elm style, used by System76's COSMIC desktop. GPU rendering (wgpu) with a software fallback (tiny-skia) |
| Lists | `scrollable` + render only the visible rows | Smooth scrolling through 100k+ rows |
| Async work (UI) | iced `Task` on tokio | Loading states for disk and network work without blocking the UI |
| App directories | `directories` (XDG) | `~/.local/share`, `~/.cache`, `~/.config`; Flatpak redirects these into its sandbox |
| Database | **SQLite** via `rusqlite` (bundled), **FTS5** for search | Local, millisecond search, zero cost |
| Steam files | `steamlocate`, `keyvalues-parser` | Finds Steam (native + Flatpak) and parses VDF/ACF |
| System info | `sysinfo` + reading `/proc`, `/sys`, `vulkaninfo` | CPU, RAM, disks, GPU details |
| HTTP | `reqwest` (rustls), only inside `crates/net` | Live lookups, images, database download |
| Serialization | `serde`, `serde_json` | Everything |
| Compression | `zstd` | Smaller database downloads |
| Tests (Rust) | built-in tests + `insta` snapshots | Parser and matcher correctness |
| Tests (UI) | `iced_test` (headless simulator) + unit tests on `update` | Screens and state changes, no display needed |
| Dependency rules | `cargo-deny` | Enforces that only `crates/net` has an HTTP client (§6) |
| Packaging | `cargo-packager` (deb, AppImage, pacman), `cargo-generate-rpm` (rpm) | Linux packages from the same binary |
| Pipeline | Rust binary in the same workspace | Shares `core` with the app |
| CI/CD | GitHub Actions | Free for public repos |

---

## 5. Repository layout

```
rigcheck/
├── Cargo.toml                 # Rust workspace
├── deny.toml                  # dependency rules (only crates/net may do HTTP)
├── app/                       # the desktop app (iced), binary `rigcheck`
│   └── src/                   # main.rs + one module per screen
├── pipeline/                  # data pipeline binary (crawl, parse, build games.db)
├── crates/                    # libraries shared by app/ and pipeline/
│   ├── core/                  # requirement parser, matcher, shared types (no I/O)
│   ├── hardware/              # Linux hardware detection
│   ├── steam/                 # Steam install + library discovery
│   ├── gamedb/                # games.db schema, queries, migrations
│   └── net/                   # HTTP client with the host allowlist (§6)
├── packaging/                 # .desktop file, AppStream metainfo, Flatpak manifest (Phase 7)
├── website/                   # Astro showcase site (Phase 9, after v1.0)
├── assets/brand/              # pixel-art icon and the scripts that draw it
├── data/                      # hand-maintained, version-controlled inputs
│   ├── hardware.toml          # known CPUs/GPUs: scores, aliases ("GTX 1060" → GTX 1060 6GB), PCI IDs
│   ├── seed/games.toml        # the seed games.db's games and Linux facts (until Phase 4)
│   └── fixtures/              # real requirement strings + fake /proc, /sys trees for tests
├── .github/workflows/
│   ├── ci.yml                 # lint + test on every PR
│   ├── release-app.yml        # build + publish app on tag
│   └── build-db.yml           # scheduled data pipeline
├── ROADMAP.md
└── README.md
```

**Rule of thumb:** things you run live at the top (`app/`, `pipeline/`), and logic lives in `crates/`. `app/` stays thin: screens, state and wiring. Anything worth unit-testing belongs in a crate.

Crate packages are prefixed (`rigcheck-core`, …) because a package called `core` would clash with Rust's built-in `core` library. Directory names stay short.

**Testability rule:** `hardware` and `steam` take a root path (default `/`, or `$HOME` for Steam). Tests point them at fake directory trees in `data/fixtures/`, so detection gets tested without real hardware.

---

## 6. Privacy & network

The app makes **only** these requests. This list goes in the README and on an in-app "Privacy" page.

| Destination | When | What is sent |
|---|---|---|
| `github.com` (Releases, files served from `release-assets.githubusercontent.com`) | On startup (configurable), to fetch `manifest.json` and, if newer, `games.db.zst`; and the latest app release's `version.txt` for the update notice | A plain file download. No identifiers |
| `store.steampowered.com/api/appdetails` | When the user opens a game missing from `games.db` | The app ID being looked up |
| Steam CDN | When showing cover art | The app ID of the image |

As with any download, GitHub and Valve see the user's IP address. The project itself receives **nothing**.

**Enforced in code, not just promised:**
- Only `crates/net` may depend on an HTTP client. `deny.toml` bans `reqwest` everywhere else (and bans other HTTP clients outright), and `cargo deny check bans` fails CI if that ever changes.
- The client in `crates/net` only accepts the three hosts above. Any other host is a bug.
- A settings toggle lets users disable automatic update checks and update manually.

---

## 7. Data design

### 7.1 Files on the user's machine (XDG)

| File | Path | Clearable? |
|---|---|---|
| `games.db` | `~/.local/share/rigcheck/` | No. The UI offers **Re-download** instead |
| `fetched.db` | `~/.cache/rigcheck/` | Yes. Holds live lookups for games not in `games.db` |
| Cover images | `~/.cache/rigcheck/images/` | Yes. LRU-evicted at a user-set limit (default 500 MB) |
| `settings.json` | `~/.config/rigcheck/` | Reset button |

Use the `directories` crate (`ProjectDirs`), which follows the XDG variables. Flatpak points those variables into the sandbox, so the same code works there.

**Lookup order:** `games.db` → `fetched.db` → live fetch (stored in `fetched.db`). Updating `games.db` never touches `fetched.db`. Entries in `fetched.db` older than 30 days, or that later appear in `games.db`, are ignored and pruned.

### 7.2 `games.db` schema (draft)

```sql
CREATE TABLE meta (key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value TEXT);
-- schema_version, built_at, source versions, attribution

CREATE TABLE games (
  app_id              INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name                TEXT NOT NULL,
  release_date        TEXT,
  popularity          INTEGER,          -- used to rank search results
  linux_native        INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  protondb_tier       TEXT,             -- platinum|gold|silver|bronze|borked|NULL
  protondb_reports    INTEGER,
  deck_status         TEXT,             -- verified|playable|unsupported|unknown
  anticheat_status    TEXT,             -- none|supported|running|planned|broken|denied|NULL
  anticheat_name      TEXT,             -- EAC, BattlEye, ...
  requirements_status TEXT NOT NULL,    -- parsed|partial|missing|not_crawled
  updated_at          INTEGER NOT NULL
);

CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE games_fts USING fts5(
  name, content='games', content_rowid='app_id', tokenize='unicode61 remove_diacritics 2'
);

CREATE TABLE requirements (
  app_id      INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES games(app_id),
  tier        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (tier IN ('minimum', 'recommended')),
  ram_mb      INTEGER,
  vram_mb     INTEGER,
  storage_mb  INTEGER,
  directx     TEXT,                     -- "11", "12"
  vulkan      TEXT,
  opengl      TEXT,
  cpu_raw     TEXT,                     -- short cleaned text, shown when matching fails
  gpu_raw     TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (app_id, tier)
);

-- "Intel i5-4460 or AMD FX-6300" → two rows (OR alternatives)
CREATE TABLE requirement_hardware (
  app_id      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  tier        TEXT NOT NULL,
  kind        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (kind IN ('cpu', 'gpu')),
  position    INTEGER NOT NULL,         -- order on the store page
  hardware_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES hardware(id)
);

CREATE TABLE hardware (
  id           INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  kind         TEXT NOT NULL,           -- cpu|gpu
  vendor       TEXT NOT NULL,           -- intel|amd|nvidia
  name         TEXT NOT NULL,           -- canonical display name
  score        INTEGER,                 -- normalized performance score
  score_source TEXT,                    -- blender-open-data|manual
  vram_mb      INTEGER,
  vulkan       TEXT,                    -- max supported Vulkan version (GPUs)
  release_year INTEGER
);

CREATE TABLE hardware_alias (alias TEXT PRIMARY KEY, hardware_id INTEGER NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE gpu_pci_id (
  vendor_id INTEGER, device_id INTEGER, hardware_id INTEGER,
  PRIMARY KEY (vendor_id, device_id)
);
```

`hardware`, `hardware_alias` and `gpu_pci_id` ship inside `games.db`, so the app's live-fetch parser has the same knowledge as the pipeline.

### 7.3 `manifest.json`

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "db_version": "2026-11-01.1",
  "built_at": "2026-11-01T04:00:00Z",
  "url": "https://github.com/Glory42/rigcheck/releases/download/db-latest/games.db.zst",
  "sha256": "…",
  "size_bytes": 15000000,
  "min_app_version": "0.4.0"
}
```

- If the app's supported `schema_version` is older than the manifest's, the app keeps its current database and asks the user to update the app.
- Update flow: download to a temp file → verify sha256 → decompress → open and run a sanity query → atomically rename over the old file. A failed update never leaves a broken database.

### 7.4 Size budget

| Part | Estimate |
|---|---|
| All games (search fields + FTS index) | ~10–20 MB |
| Parsed requirements | ~20 MB |
| Hardware tables, ProtonDB, anti-cheat | < 2 MB |
| **On disk** | **~30–60 MB** |
| **Download (zstd)** | **~10–20 MB** |

**Rule:** don't ship raw requirement HTML. It would add hundreds of MB. Store only the short cleaned `cpu_raw` / `gpu_raw` text, and fetch full text live if a game page needs it. A CI check fails the build if `games.db.zst` grows past a set budget (start at 50 MB).

---

## 8. Matching logic

### 8.1 Detecting the user's hardware
| Component | Source | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| CPU | `/proc/cpuinfo` model name → `hardware_alias` | Normalize ("Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-8400 CPU @ 2.80GHz" → "i5-8400") |
| GPU | `/sys/class/drm/card*/device/{vendor,device}` → `gpu_pci_id` | PCI IDs are exact, which beats matching name strings |
| VRAM | `mem_info_vram_total` (AMD), `nvidia-smi` (NVIDIA), unknown for Intel iGPUs | iGPUs share system RAM. Treat VRAM as "shared" |
| RAM | `/proc/meminfo` | Compare with 10% tolerance: the kernel and an iGPU keep some RAM, so a 16 GB laptop reports ~15.0 GiB |
| Driver | `/sys/module/nvidia/version`, Mesa version via `vulkaninfo` | Detect `nouveau` and warn about it |
| Vulkan | `vulkaninfo --summary` | If it's missing, show a "Install vulkan-tools" hint |
| Disk | Free space on the Steam library folders | |
| Distro / kernel | `/etc/os-release`, `uname` | Shown for information only |

**Hybrid laptops** (Intel/AMD iGPU + NVIDIA/AMD dGPU): detect all GPUs, use the **strongest** one for verdicts, and mention PRIME offload if relevant.

**Manual override:** users can correct detected hardware or pick "what if I had GPU X?". This also powers the "should I upgrade?" feature (§10 Phase 8).

### 8.2 Parsing requirements
1. Clean the HTML → split into fields (OS, Processor, Memory, Graphics, DirectX, Storage).
2. Split alternatives on `/`, `or`, `,`, `|`.
3. Normalize each token: lowercase, strip marketing words ("NVIDIA GeForce", "or better", "equivalent", "series"), and keep the VRAM hint ("2GB").
4. Look up in `hardware_alias`. Exact match first, then fuzzy matching with a conservative threshold.
5. Anything unmatched → record it as unknown and keep the raw text. In the pipeline, log unmatched tokens to a report so the aliases in `data/hardware.toml` can grow over time.

### 8.3 Comparing
- **CPU/GPU:** the requirement is met if `user.score >= required.score`. When several alternatives are listed ("i5-4460 or FX-6300"), compare against the **same-vendor** alternative if there is one, otherwise the lowest-scored one. *(This is a decision to revisit with real data.)*
- **RAM:** 10% tolerance (see §8.1). **VRAM and storage:** exact. A GPU that shares system RAM skips the VRAM check.
- **Graphics API:** DirectX through Proton needs Vulkan 1.3 (DXVK for DX9–11, VKD3D-Proton for DX12). Native Linux games skip this check. *(Later: driver-specific DX12 features, native OpenGL/Vulkan versions.)*
- **Confidence:** High when CPU, GPU and RAM could all be compared, Partial when some could, Low when none.
- **Proton margin:** optionally require ~10% more score for non-native games. This is a setting, off by default until it's proven useful.
- **Linux layer:** anti-cheat `denied`/`broken` → ⛔. ProtonDB `borked` → ⛔. `nouveau` driver → warning on every 3D game.

### 8.4 Output (shared Rust type, used directly by the UI)
```rust
struct Verdict {
    overall: Level,                 // Recommended | Minimum | Below | Blocked | Unknown
    components: Vec<ComponentResult>, // per CPU/GPU/RAM/VRAM/Storage/API
    bottleneck: Option<Component>,
    linux: LinuxStatus,             // proton tier, anticheat, deck, native, driver warnings
    confidence: Confidence,         // High | Partial | Low, based on how much was parsed
}
```

## 9. Data sources & licenses

| Data | Source | Access | License (verify before release) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Steam app list | `IStoreService/GetAppList` | Free Steam Web API key, stored as a GitHub Actions secret | Steam API Terms |
| Requirements | Steam `appdetails` (unofficial) | No key. ~200 requests / 5 min | Steam API Terms |
| Requirements (backup) | PCGamingWiki API | Free | CC BY-NC-SA. Check compatibility |
| Proton compatibility | ProtonDB data dumps (`bdefore/protondb-data`) | GitHub | ODbL (attribution + share-alike) |
| Anti-cheat | AreWeAntiCheatYet (GitHub JSON) | GitHub | MIT ✅ (keep the copyright notice in Credits) |
| Deck status | Steam's Deck compatibility report (`saleaction/ajaxgetdeckappcompatibilityreport`) | Unofficial, one request per game | Steam API Terms |
| CPU/GPU scores | Hand-estimated in `data/hardware.toml`; gaps from Blender Open Data | Daily snapshot | CC0 ✅ |
| PCI IDs | `pci.ids` | Public | BSD-3 / GPL-2 |
| Popularity | ProtonDB report counts, Steam's most-played charts | Free | n/a |
| App icon / logo | Original pixel art in `assets/brand/` (drawn by scripts in `assets/brand/src/`) | n/a | MIT, our own work: no attribution needed, and it can be trademarked later |

**ProtonDB tiers.** The dump has raw reports but no Platinum/Gold/… tier, and ProtonDB's formula isn't published, so rigcheck uses its own rule and the app labels it as derived from ProtonDB reports. Per report: Borked if the verdict is "no"; Bronze with stability faults or significant bugs; Silver with any other fault; Gold if it needed tweaks (didn't work out of the box, custom or GE Proton, launch options); else Platinum. Per game: the most common rating among reports from the last 12 months, or all reports if fewer than 3 are that recent; ties go to the worse tier. Reports on native Linux builds count toward popularity but not the tier.

**Hardware scores.** Hand scores in `data/hardware.toml` always win; the `report` command shows which missing parts matter most. Blender Open Data only fills gaps: a device's score is the median (≥ 3 runs) of its summed samples/minute over the three standard scenes, rescaled by the median our/Blender ratio of the 3 same-vendor table parts with the closest Blender scores (13% median error leave-one-out, against 21% for one ratio per vendor). NVIDIA uses CUDA runs, since OptiX also uses RT cores and overrates RTX cards. Blender measures rendering, not games, so these scores are lower confidence: CPUs with many cores and older GTX cards are the least accurate.

**Rules:**
- An in-app **Credits** page lists every source with its license.
- `games.db` is published under ODbL (see §1.2), and the code under MIT.
- Be polite: honor rate limits, send a descriptive `User-Agent` with the repo URL, cache everything and never re-crawl unchanged games.

## 10. Phases

Each phase ends with a usable, tested result. Check items off as you go.

### Phase 0: Foundation (v0.0)
- [x] Install the toolchain: `rustup` (stable, with clippy and rustfmt) and `cargo-deny`. iced loads Wayland/X11/Vulkan at runtime, so there are no extra system packages to build
- [ ] Learn Rust basics: *The Rust Book*, chapters 1–10. Keep going in parallel; you don't have to finish first
- [x] Create a **private** GitHub repo (`Glory42/rigcheck`) with the MIT license (see §1.1)
- [x] Set up the Cargo workspace and the crate skeletons from §5
- [x] iced app skeleton in `app/` that opens an empty window with the brand icon, plus a headless `iced_test` test
- [x] CI (`ci.yml`): `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -D warnings`, `cargo test`, `cargo deny check bans`. Run on `master` + PRs only, with Rust caching, to stay inside the private-repo minutes
- [x] Network lock: `crates/net` skeleton, and a `deny.toml` that bans HTTP clients from every other crate (§6)

**Done when:** an empty app window opens, and CI passes on a pull request.

### Phase 1: My Library (v0.1)
- [x] `steam` crate: find Steam installs (native `~/.steam`, `~/.local/share/Steam`, Flatpak `~/.var/app/com.valvesoftware.Steam`)
- [x] Parse `libraryfolders.vdf` → all library folders (including other drives)
- [x] Parse `appmanifest_*.acf` → app ID, name, install size, folder
- [x] Filter out non-games (Proton versions, Steam Linux Runtime, Steamworks redistributables)
- [x] Load installed games into the app with an iced `Task`, so the scan never blocks the UI
- [x] Cover art from Steam's own cache on disk (`steam::cover_art`), shown with iced's `image` widget. Nothing is downloaded; CDN downloads for uncached games move to Phase 5
- [x] Library page: grid of cover tiles with name, verdict stamp and search box (a plain grid is fast enough for an installed library; the Catalog's 100k games get virtualization in Phase 5)
- [x] Tests with fixture Steam directories

**Done when:** the app shows your installed Steam games with cover art, including games on secondary drives.

### Phase 2: My Hardware (v0.2)
- [x] `hardware` crate: CPU, RAM, GPU(s) via PCI IDs, VRAM, driver, Vulkan, disk, distro/kernel (§8.1)
- [x] Handle hybrid GPUs, iGPU-only systems, `nouveau`, and a missing `vulkaninfo`
- [x] Fixture tests: fake `/proc` + `/sys` trees for an AMD desktop, an NVIDIA desktop, an Intel laptop, a hybrid laptop and a Steam Deck
- [x] My Hardware page with a "Copy as text" button (useful for asking for help; copying stays local)
- [x] Manual hardware override UI: type to pick a GPU/CPU from the hardware table on My Rig; saved, and verdicts use it

**Done when:** the hardware page is correct on your machine and every fixture test passes.

### Phase 3: Matcher core (v0.3)
Build this test-first. It's pure logic with no I/O, so it's the easiest part to get right with tests.
- [x] `core` types: `Requirement`, `HardwareRef`, `Verdict`, `Level`, `Confidence`
- [x] Requirement parser (§8.2 step 1): fields, RAM/VRAM/storage/DirectX numbers, with a fixture corpus of **100+ real requirement strings** (145 games, 268 tiers, 92.9% fully parsed) and snapshot tests (`insta`)
- [x] Match CPU/GPU text to the hardware table (§8.2 steps 2–5): split alternatives, normalize, alias lookup (fuzzy matching later)
- [x] Matcher (§8.3), with tests covering every verdict level and edge case
- [x] Hand-write a **seed `games.db`** with ~20 games covering the range: native Linux, Proton Platinum, anti-cheat denied, DX12-heavy, ancient, brand new, missing requirements (`data/seed/games.toml`, 22 games)
- [x] Seed hardware table with ~50 common CPUs/GPUs, using manual scores for now (`data/hardware.toml`, ~70 entries)
- [x] Verdict badges on the Library page, and a first version of the game page

**Done when:** your installed games that appear in the seed DB show correct verdicts, and the parser corpus is ≥ 90% parsed.

### Phase 4: Data pipeline v1 (v0.4)
- [x] **Make the repo public** (checklist in §1.1). This is required for free scheduled Actions and public `games.db` downloads
- [x] Add the `games.db` ODbL license notice and the Credits data (§9): `build` writes both into games.db's `meta` table; the app's Credits page is Phase 7
- [x] `pipeline` binary with subcommands: `applist`, `crawl`, `build` (which does the enriching), `validate`, `report`
- [x] App list: fetch every app → keep games and drop DLC, soundtracks, tools and demos
- [x] Crawler: rate-limited (stay under the limit), retries with backoff, **resumable**. State lives in the previous `games.db` (`crawl_log`: when each app was fetched), so each run continues where the last one stopped, and unchanged store pages aren't fetched again
- [x] Crawl priority: popular first (by ProtonDB report count), then the most recently changed store pages
- [x] Enrich: ProtonDB dump (tiers by our own rule, see §9) and AreWeAntiCheatYet
- [x] Enrich: Deck status (one store request per game), hardware scores (hand scores in `data/hardware.toml` first; Blender Open Data fills parts the table lacks, see §9), GPU PCI IDs from `pci.ids`
- [x] `validate`: size budget and sanity checks: not empty, and ≥ 90% of the 100 most popular games parsed (not 100%: some popular games leave a field out on Steam, e.g. TF2 lists no GPU)
- [x] `report`: unmatched hardware tokens sorted by frequency, used to grow the aliases in `data/hardware.toml`
- [x] `build-db.yml`: daily cron → download the previous release → run the pipeline (stop well under the 6-hour job limit) → publish `games.db.zst` + `manifest.json` to a rolling `db-latest` release
- [x] Keep scheduled workflows alive: GitHub disables cron in repos inactive for 60 days, so each run re-enables its own workflow through the API (a commit would need a pull request, since `master` is protected)
- [ ] Optional: run the first full crawl locally to get past the multi-day backlog faster

**Done when:** a scheduled run publishes a valid `games.db` with the top ~5k games fully parsed and every game searchable by name.

### Phase 5: Catalog & live lookups (v0.5)
- [x] App downloads `games.db` on first launch, with a progress bar. The download is checked (SHA-256, then a sanity query) before it replaces anything; offline, the app says so and offers Retry. The built-in seed is now test data only
- [x] Catalog page: FTS5 search, ranked by popularity, with a virtualized list (only the rows in view are fetched and drawn; the popularity index is built on install instead of shipped). Rows open the game page; games known only by name say NOT CHECKED YET
- [x] Filters: "Only games I can run", ProtonDB tier, native Linux, Deck verified, no anti-cheat issues. ProtonDB keeps a tier or better; anti-cheat issues are Denied, Broken and Planned. CAN RUN works out every checked game's verdict in bulk (~90 ms for 3k games), once per set of specs; at ~70k checked games that becomes ~2 s, so it should move off the UI thread before then
- [x] Full game page: per-component table (each row says how your PC compares), bottleneck, Linux status, raw requirement text and a link to the Steam store page. The text is kept in games.db (`requirements.text`, ~620 bytes a game); games crawled before that are re-crawled once. The store link opens in the user's browser through `xdg-open`, so the app itself sends nothing
- [x] `fetch` module: live `appdetails` lookup for games missing from `games.db` or with `not_crawled` status → parse with `core` → store in `fetched.db` (`app/src/lookup.rs`; ingest now lives in `gamedb`, shared with the pipeline). Asked when the game's page opens; the lookup keeps the ProtonDB/anti-cheat/Deck facts games.db has, and is asked again after 30 days. Not done yet: pruning old `fetched.db` rows, and Catalog rows still say NOT CHECKED YET for looked-up games
- [x] Client-side rate limiting and a clear "couldn't reach Steam" state: one shared client, 20 lookups a minute (Steam allows ~200 per 5 minutes), one retry on 429/5xx; offline shows "Couldn't reach Steam." with RETRY, and DLC or delisted apps say Steam lists no requirements
- [x] Cover art from the Steam CDN (via `crates/net`, cached in `~/.cache/rigcheck/images/`) for games Steam hasn't cached locally (`app/src/covers.rs`: Steam's own cache wins; each cover asked for at most once a session; 10 a second)

**Done when:** you can search any Steam game, open it and get a verdict, including games the pipeline hasn't crawled yet.

### Phase 6: Updates & storage (v0.6)
- [x] Updater: manifest check → download → verify → atomic swap (§7.3). At every start unless turned off (`manual_updates`); installs record their `db_version`, and any other published build counts as an update. Killed by hand at 2.5 of 6.8 MB: the old games.db kept working and the next start installed cleanly
- [x] Schema version check and a "please update the app" message (the current games.db stays in use)
- [x] Settings → Storage: sizes, Check for updates, Re-download database, Clear fetched games, Clear images, image cache limit (100 MB, 250 MB, 500 MB default, 1 GB)
- [x] Settings → Privacy: auto-update toggle and the list of network destinations (§6)
- [x] LRU image cache eviction: showing a downloaded cover marks it used; the least recently used go first, at start and after every download. Steam's own cache is never touched

**Done when:** the database updates in the background with no broken states, even if you kill the app mid-download (test that).

### Phase 7: Packaging & release (v0.7)
- [x] `release-app.yml`: on tag → build AppImage, `.deb`, `.rpm` and a tarball → attach to a GitHub Release. Uses `cargo-deb`, `cargo-generate-rpm` and `appimagetool` on a hand-made AppDir instead of `cargo-packager`, so every package installs our own `.desktop` file, metainfo and icons. Pull requests touching packaging build them too
- [x] Update notice: compare the running version with the latest GitHub Release and link to it (each release uploads `version.txt`; `releases/latest/download/version.txt` skips the `db-latest` prerelease). Flathub and AUR users get updates from their package manager, so the app never replaces its own binary
- [ ] Test on at least Arch, Ubuntu/Debian, Fedora and SteamOS (Deck desktop mode)
- [ ] Test on NVIDIA proprietary drivers and on a machine without working Vulkan. iced should fall back to its software renderer (tiny-skia); check that it does
- [ ] AUR package (`rigcheck-bin`): `packaging/aur/PKGBUILD` is ready and builds with `makepkg`; publishing needs the maintainer's AUR account
- [ ] Flathub submission (manifest, permissions: read-only access to Steam folders and network). The manifest is in `packaging/flatpak/`; generating `cargo-sources.json`, a local `flatpak-builder` run and the submission are left (packaging/README.md)
- [x] Desktop integration in `packaging/`: a `.desktop` file named after the app ID (`dev.gorkemkaryol.rigcheck`), AppStream metainfo, and hicolor icons (`128`, `256`, `512` from `assets/brand/`). On Wayland, the window icon comes from this `.desktop` file. CI validates both files
- [x] About page in the app: version, license, links, data-source credits (§9)
- [x] README with screenshots, privacy section and credits (screenshots rendered offscreen by `app/src/screenshots.rs`)

**Done when:** a stranger can install the app from Flathub or AUR and it works.

### Phase 8: Polish → v1.0
- [x] "What if I upgrade?": pick a hypothetical GPU/CPU/RAM and see which games change verdict (My Rig; installed games, nothing saved)
- [x] Library summary: "38 of 42 installed games meet recommended specs"
- [x] Sort and group the library by verdict (A–Z, or grouped READY → LOW → TOO WEAK → BLOCKED → ??? → NOT CHECKED YET → NO DATA)
- [x] Compare two games side by side (COMPARE on one game page, COMPARE WITH … on another: verdicts, each part's minimum and result, Linux facts)
- [x] Keyboard navigation and accessibility pass: Ctrl+1…5 tabs, Ctrl+F search, Enter opens, ↑/↓/Page keys walk the Catalog, Esc goes back (listed on About); every appearance passes WCAG AA contrast (tested). Not possible yet: screen readers, since iced 0.14 has no accessibility tree (AccessKit)
- [x] Light/dark theme following the system (SYSTEM, the default: Paper when light, Ink when dark, switching live)
- [x] Performance pass: cold start under 1 s, search under 50 ms on 100k games. Measured on ~198k games (`app/src/perf.rs`, Ryzen 5 7530U): start-up work, hardware detection, Steam scan and first view 163 ms (the window and GPU setup aren't included); "s" (50k matches) 29 ms, from 88 ms. Install builds a name search with 1–3 letter prefix indexes (~6 s, +13 MB on disk); broad queries walk the popularity index; a plain search counts on the search table alone
- [ ] Tune the parser against the `report` output until ≥ 95% of the top 5k games parse fully

**Done when:** v1.0 is tagged, and a post on r/linux_gaming doesn't surface show-stopping bugs.

### Phase 9: Showcase website (after v1.0)
A static showcase page. It describes the app and sends people to GitHub, Flathub or AUR. It has no backend, collects no data and runs no analytics.
- [ ] Astro site in `apps/website/`
- [ ] Host on a subdomain of `gorkemkaryol.dev` (e.g. `rigcheck.gorkemkaryol.dev`)
- [ ] Free hosting: GitHub Pages (custom domain via a `CNAME` DNS record) or Cloudflare Pages
- [ ] Content: what it does, screenshots or a short video, privacy promise (§6), install buttons (Flathub, AUR, AppImage/deb/rpm from GitHub Releases), credits
- [ ] Favicon from `assets/brand/` (`icon-16.png`, `icon-32.png`, `icon-64.png`)
- [ ] Optional: a "latest version" badge, read at build time from the GitHub Releases API

**Done when:** the subdomain serves the page over HTTPS and every install link works.

## 11. Future ideas (post-1.0, only if they keep the principles)

- **Owned games:** an optional Steam Web API key entered by the user, stored locally and only ever sent to Steam.
- **Non-Steam launchers:** Heroic (GOG/Epic) and Lutris libraries, read from local config files. Requirements would come from PCGamingWiki.
- **Wishlist import:** paste a Steam wishlist URL to see which wishlisted games you can run.
- **Translations** (i18n).
- **Diff-based database updates** if `games.db` ever grows past ~100 MB.
- **CLI companion** (`rigcheck check "elden ring"`), which is easy since all the logic is in Rust crates.

## 12. Risks & mitigations

| Risk | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Steam changes or blocks the unofficial `appdetails` endpoint | Pipeline and live lookups break | Cache aggressively, use PCGamingWiki as a backup, and keep the pipeline's sources modular |
| Requirement parsing is inaccurate | Wrong verdicts erode trust | Show ❓ instead of guessing, use a large fixture corpus, track parse-rate metrics in `report`, show raw text on every game page |
| Hardware scores missing for old or obscure parts | Unknown verdicts | Manual scores in `data/hardware.toml`, fall back to a release-year/tier estimate marked "low confidence" |
| iced is pre-1.0 | Breaking changes between releases, weaker screen-reader support than GTK or the web | Pin the version, keep `app/` thin so upgrades touch little code, upgrade on purpose rather than automatically |
| GPU driver problems (no Vulkan, old drivers) | Blank or crashing window for some users | iced falls back to software rendering (tiny-skia). Document `ICED_BACKEND=tiny-skia` and test on NVIDIA every release |
| Scheduled workflow auto-disabled | Database goes stale | The pipeline commits a version file each run, and a "DB older than 7 days" warning appears in the app |
| Steam installed via Flatpak or Snap | Library not found | Check all known paths, plus a manual "add Steam folder" option |
| First crawl takes days | Slow start | Crawl popular games first, make it resumable, and optionally run the first crawl locally |
| Data license conflicts | Legal risk | Verify every license in §9 before v0.4. Keep attribution in the app and the database `meta` table |
| Private-repo Actions minutes run out (2,000/month) | CI blocked during Phases 0–3 | CI only on `master` + PRs with Rust caching, no scheduled jobs while private, go public before Phase 4 |
| Learning Rust while building | Slow progress | Phases 1–3 need only basic Rust. Keep the `core` crate pure and test-driven, and don't optimize early. For the UI, start each screen from the closest iced example |

## 13. Zero-cost checklist

| Need | Free solution |
|---|---|
| Code hosting | Public GitHub repo |
| CI/CD and pipeline compute | GitHub Actions (free for public repos) |
| Database hosting | GitHub Releases asset (up to 2 GB per file) |
| App distribution | GitHub Releases, Flathub, AUR |
| App updates | Flathub and AUR, plus an in-app "new version" notice from GitHub Releases |
| Code signing | Not required on Linux. The updater key is self-generated |
| Images | Steam CDN directly |
| Steam Web API key | Free |
| Website (after v1.0) | GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages on a subdomain of `gorkemkaryol.dev` (domain already owned) |
| Servers, databases, analytics | **None. That's the point** |

## 14. Learning resources

- *The Rust Book*: https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/
- *Rust by Example*: https://doc.rust-lang.org/rust-by-example/
- iced book and API docs: https://book.iced.rs/, https://docs.rs/iced
- iced examples (most features have one): https://github.com/iced-rs/iced/tree/master/examples
- cargo-deny: https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/
- `rusqlite` docs + the SQLite FTS5 docs: https://www.sqlite.org/fts5.html
- Steam VDF/ACF format: Valve Developer Community wiki ("KeyValues")
- Linux sysfs for DRM devices: kernel documentation, `/sys/class/drm`

`SECURITY.md`:

```md
# Security

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please report security problems privately, not in a public issue:

- **Preferred:** GitHub's [private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/Glory42/rigcheck/security/advisories/new) (Security tab → "Report a vulnerability").
- **Or email** [me@gorkemkaryol.dev](mailto:me@gorkemkaryol.dev).

Include what you found, how to reproduce it, and what an attacker could do with it. I aim to reply within a week. Once a fix is released, you'll be credited in the advisory unless you'd rather not be.

rigcheck is a one-person side project, so there's no bug bounty.

## Supported versions

Before v1.0, only the latest release gets fixes.

## What's in scope

rigcheck runs on your machine with your user's permissions. The parts worth a close look:

| Area | What it does |
|---|---|
| Files it reads | `/proc`, `/sys`, `/etc/os-release`, and Steam's folders (`libraryfolders.vdf`, app manifests, cached cover art) |
| Programs it runs | `vulkaninfo --summary` and `nvidia-smi` from `PATH` |
| Files it writes | `~/.config/rigcheck/settings.json` and `~/.local/share/rigcheck/games.db` |
| Network | None today. Later versions talk to exactly three read-only destinations (GitHub Releases, Steam's store API, Steam's image CDN), all through `crates/net`; see [ROADMAP §6](ROADMAP.md#6-privacy--network) |

Especially interesting: anything that makes the app talk to another host, run another program, or read or write outside the paths above, and anything in a downloaded `games.db` or Steam file that can do more than produce a wrong verdict.

Wrong verdicts themselves aren't security issues. Report them as a [Wrong verdict](https://github.com/Glory42/rigcheck/issues/new?template=wrong-verdict.yml) issue.

```

`app/Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[package]
name = "rigcheck"
description = "Can my PC run this game? A Linux desktop app for Steam."
version.workspace = true
edition.workspace = true
license.workspace = true
publish.workspace = true
homepage = "https://github.com/Glory42/rigcheck"
repository = "https://github.com/Glory42/rigcheck"

[dependencies]
directories = "6.0.0"
fluent-bundle = "0.16"
# `image` decodes the PNG window icon now and cover art later.
iced = { version = "0.14", features = ["image"] }
rigcheck-core = { version = "0.7.0", path = "../crates/core" }
rigcheck-gamedb = { version = "0.7.0", path = "../crates/gamedb" }
rigcheck-hardware = { path = "../crates/hardware" }
rigcheck-net = { version = "0.7.0", path = "../crates/net" }
rigcheck-steam = { version = "0.7.0", path = "../crates/steam" }
serde = { version = "1.0.229", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1.0.154"
unic-langid = "0.9"

[dev-dependencies]
iced_test = "0.14"
tempfile = "3.27.0"

# `cargo deb` (packaging/README.md). Paths are relative to this crate;
# target/release/rigcheck is found in the workspace target dir.
[package.metadata.deb]
name = "rigcheck"
maintainer = "Glory42 <https://github.com/Glory42>"
section = "games"
extended-description = "Checks Steam games against your PC's hardware: ProtonDB, anti-cheat, Steam Deck status and which part holds a game back. Local-first, no telemetry."
depends = "$auto"
assets = [
    ["target/release/rigcheck", "usr/bin/", "755"],
    ["../packaging/dev.gorkemkaryol.rigcheck.desktop", "usr/share/applications/", "644"],
    ["../packaging/dev.gorkemkaryol.rigcheck.metainfo.xml", "usr/share/metainfo/", "644"],
    ["../assets/brand/icon-128.png", "usr/share/icons/hicolor/128x128/apps/dev.gorkemkaryol.rigcheck.png", "644"],
    ["../assets/brand/icon-256.png", "usr/share/icons/hicolor/256x256/apps/dev.gorkemkaryol.rigcheck.png", "644"],
    ["../assets/brand/icon-512.png", "usr/share/icons/hicolor/512x512/apps/dev.gorkemkaryol.rigcheck.png", "644"],
]

# `cargo generate-rpm`, the same files.
[package.metadata.generate-rpm]
assets = [
    { source = "target/release/rigcheck", dest = "/usr/bin/rigcheck", mode = "755" },
    { source = "../packaging/dev.gorkemkaryol.rigcheck.desktop", dest = "/usr/share/applications/dev.gorkemkaryol.rigcheck.desktop", mode = "644" },
    { source = "../packaging/dev.gorkemkaryol.rigcheck.metainfo.xml", dest = "/usr/share/metainfo/dev.gorkemkaryol.rigcheck.metainfo.xml", mode = "644" },
    { source = "../assets/brand/icon-128.png", dest = "/usr/share/icons/hicolor/128x128/apps/dev.gorkemkaryol.rigcheck.png", mode = "644" },
    { source = "../assets/brand/icon-256.png", dest = "/usr/share/icons/hicolor/256x256/apps/dev.gorkemkaryol.rigcheck.png", mode = "644" },
    { source = "../assets/brand/icon-512.png", dest = "/usr/share/icons/hicolor/512x512/apps/dev.gorkemkaryol.rigcheck.png", mode = "644" },
]


```

`app/src/catalog.rs`:

```rs
//! The Catalog page: every game in games.db, most popular first, searchable.
//! The list is virtual: only the rows in view are fetched and drawn.

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::ops::Range;

use iced::widget::{button, column, container, row, scrollable, space, text, text_input};
use iced::{Element, Fill};
use rigcheck_core::{ProtonTier, Specs};
use rigcheck_gamedb::{Filters, Game, GameDb};

use crate::i18n::I18n;
use crate::library::{Status, stamp, status};
use crate::style::{BOLD, Colors};
use crate::{Message, Page};

/// The search box's and the list's widget IDs.
pub const SEARCH: &str = "catalog-search";
pub const LIST: &str = "catalog-list";

/// Every row is this tall, so a scroll position maps straight to rows.
pub const ROW_HEIGHT: f32 = 48.0;

/// A filter that's on or off.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Chip {
    /// Only games this PC (with any override) reaches the minimum for.
    CanRun,
    NativeLinux,
    DeckVerified,
    NoAntiCheatIssues,
}

impl Chip {
    const ALL: [Chip; 4] = [
        Chip::CanRun,
        Chip::NativeLinux,
        Chip::DeckVerified,
        Chip::NoAntiCheatIssues,
    ];

    fn label_id(self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            Chip::CanRun => "filter-can-run",
            Chip::NativeLinux => "filter-native-linux",
            Chip::DeckVerified => "filter-deck-verified",
            Chip::NoAntiCheatIssues => "filter-no-anticheat-issues",
        }
    }

    fn is_on(self, list: &List) -> bool {
        match self {
            Chip::CanRun => list.can_run,
            Chip::NativeLinux => list.filters.native_linux,
            Chip::DeckVerified => list.filters.deck_verified,
            Chip::NoAntiCheatIssues => list.filters.no_anticheat_issues,
        }
    }
}

/// The list's state: what's searched, where it's scrolled, and the rows in
/// view (fetched from games.db as they come into view).
pub struct List {
    query: String,
    filters: Filters,
    /// Whether CAN RUN is on. `filters.runs_on` holds the specs it uses
    /// once hardware detection has finished.
    can_run: bool,
    scroll: f32,
    viewport: f32,
    total: usize,
    /// The index of `rows[0]` in the whole list.
    first: usize,
    /// The row the keyboard has highlighted.
    selected: usize,
    rows: Vec<Game>,
}

impl Default for List {
    fn default() -> List {
        List {
            query: String::new(),
            filters: Filters::default(),
            can_run: false,
            scroll: 0.0,
            // Until the list reports its size: enough for a tall window.
            viewport: 1200.0,
            total: 0,
            first: 0,
            selected: 0,
            rows: Vec::new(),
        }
    }
}

impl List {
    /// Fetches the rows that scrolled into view. The count stays: it
    /// only changes with the search (and costs ~30 ms on a broad one).
    pub fn scrolled(&mut self, offset: f32, height: f32, db: &GameDb) {
        self.scroll = offset;
        self.viewport = height;
        self.fetch_rows(db);
    }

    /// Lists `query`'s matches from the top. The caller scrolls the list
    /// widget back up too ([`LIST`]), as for every change of what's listed.
    pub fn search(&mut self, query: String, db: &GameDb) {
        self.query = query;
        self.restart(db);
    }

    /// Turns `chip` on or off. `specs` are this PC's, for CAN RUN.
    pub fn toggle(&mut self, chip: Chip, specs: Option<Specs>, db: &GameDb) {
        let on = !chip.is_on(self);
        match chip {
            Chip::CanRun => {
                self.can_run = on;
                self.filters.runs_on = specs.filter(|_| on);
            }
            Chip::NativeLinux => self.filters.native_linux = on,
            Chip::DeckVerified => self.filters.deck_verified = on,
            Chip::NoAntiCheatIssues => self.filters.no_anticheat_issues = on,
        }
        self.restart(db);
    }

    /// Keeps games ProtonDB rates `lowest` or better; `None` keeps all.
    pub fn protondb(&mut self, lowest: Option<ProtonTier>, db: &GameDb) {
        self.filters.protondb_at_least = lowest;
        self.restart(db);
    }

    /// Uses new specs (detection finished, or an override changed) for
    /// CAN RUN, if it's on.
    pub fn use_specs(&mut self, specs: Option<Specs>, db: &GameDb) {
        if self.can_run && self.filters.runs_on != specs {
            self.filters.runs_on = specs;
            self.restart(db);
        }
    }

    /// Lists from the first row again, after what's listed changed.
    fn restart(&mut self, db: &GameDb) {
        self.scroll = 0.0;
        self.selected = 0;
        self.refresh(db);
    }

    /// Counts the matches and fetches the rows in view, e.g. for a new games.db.
    pub fn refresh(&mut self, db: &GameDb) {
        self.total = db.games_count(&self.query, &self.filters).unwrap_or(0);
        self.rows.clear();
        self.fetch_rows(db);
    }

    /// Moves the highlight `by` rows and scrolls it into view. Returns the
    /// new scroll offset, for the caller to move the list widget too.
    pub fn move_selection(&mut self, by: i32, db: &GameDb) -> f32 {
        if self.total == 0 {
            return self.scroll;
        }
        let last = self.total - 1;
        self.selected = (self.selected as i64 + i64::from(by)).clamp(0, last as i64) as usize;
        let top = self.selected as f32 * ROW_HEIGHT;
        if top < self.scroll {
            self.scroll = top;
        } else if top + ROW_HEIGHT > self.scroll + self.viewport {
            self.scroll = top + ROW_HEIGHT - self.viewport;
        }
        self.fetch_rows(db);
        self.scroll
    }

    /// The highlighted game's app ID.
    pub fn selected_game(&self, db: &GameDb) -> Option<u32> {
        match self.selected.checked_sub(self.first) {
            Some(index) if index < self.rows.len() => Some(self.rows[index].app_id),
            _ => db
                .games_page(&self.query, &self.filters, self.selected, 1)
                .ok()?
                .first()
                .map(|(app_id, _)| *app_id),
        }
    }

    fn fetch_rows(&mut self, db: &GameDb) {
        let range = visible_rows(self.scroll, self.viewport, ROW_HEIGHT, self.total);
        if range.start == self.first && range.len() == self.rows.len() && !self.rows.is_empty() {
            return; // Same rows as before.
        }
        let page = db
            .games_page(&self.query, &self.filters, range.start, range.len())
            .unwrap_or_default();
        self.first = range.start;
        // Scrolling a little keeps most rows: reuse them and only load the
        // records that came into view (a full record takes ~1.5 ms).
        let mut loaded: HashMap<u32, Game> = self
            .rows
            .drain(..)
            .map(|game| (game.app_id, game))
            .collect();
        self.rows = page
            .into_iter()
            .filter_map(|(app_id, _)| {
                loaded
                    .remove(&app_id)
                    .or_else(|| db.game(app_id).ok().flatten())
            })
            .collect();
    }
}

/// `specs` is `None` until hardware detection finishes.
pub fn view<'a>(
    list: &'a List,
    specs: Option<&Specs>,
    i18n: &I18n,
    colors: Colors,
) -> Element<'a, Message> {
    let above = list.first as f32 * ROW_HEIGHT;
    let below = list.total.saturating_sub(list.first + list.rows.len()) as f32 * ROW_HEIGHT;
    let rows = list.rows.iter().enumerate().map(|(index, game)| {
        let selected = list.first + index == list.selected;
        game_row(game, &status(Some(game), specs), selected, i18n, colors)
    });
    let search_box = text_input(&i18n.t("catalog-search"), &list.query)
        .id(SEARCH)
        .on_input(Message::CatalogSearch)
        // Enter opens the highlighted row (the first, after a new search).
        .on_submit(Message::Shortcut(crate::keys::Shortcut::Open))
        .padding(10)
        .font(BOLD);
    let list_view = scrollable(
        column![space().height(above)]
            .extend(rows)
            .push(space().height(below))
            .width(Fill),
    )
    .on_scroll(|viewport| Message::CatalogScrolled {
        offset: viewport.absolute_offset().y,
        height: viewport.bounds().height,
    })
    .id(LIST)
    .height(Fill);
    let chips = Chip::ALL.map(|chip| {
        button(text(i18n.t(chip.label_id())).font(BOLD).size(12))
            .padding([6, 10])
            .style(colors.button(chip.is_on(list)))
            // CAN RUN needs the hardware first.
            .on_press_maybe(
                (chip != Chip::CanRun || specs.is_some()).then_some(Message::CatalogFilter(chip)),
            )
            .into()
    });
    let tier_button = |lowest: Option<ProtonTier>| {
        let label = match lowest {
            None => i18n.t("filter-protondb-any"),
            // ProtonDB's own tier names, as on the game page.
            Some(ProtonTier::Platinum) => "PLATINUM".to_owned(),
            Some(tier) => format!("{}+", format!("{tier:?}").to_uppercase()),
        };
        button(text(label).font(BOLD).size(12))
            .padding([6, 10])
            .style(colors.button(list.filters.protondb_at_least == lowest))
            .on_press(Message::CatalogProtonDb(lowest))
            .into()
    };
    let tiers = row![text(i18n.t("game-protondb")).font(BOLD).size(12)]
        .extend(
            [
                None,
                Some(ProtonTier::Platinum),
                Some(ProtonTier::Gold),
                Some(ProtonTier::Silver),
                Some(ProtonTier::Bronze),
            ]
            .map(tier_button),
        )
        .spacing(8)
        .align_y(iced::Center);
    column![search_box, row(chips).spacing(8).wrap(), tiers, list_view]
        .spacing(16)
        .into()
}

fn game_row<'a>(
    game: &'a Game,
    status: &Status,
    // Highlighted for the keyboard.
    selected: bool,
    i18n: &I18n,
    colors: Colors,
) -> Element<'a, Message> {
    let (label, color) = stamp(status, i18n);
    let stamp = container(text(label).font(BOLD).size(12))
        .padding([3, 8])
        .style(move |_| container::Style {
            text_color: Some(colors.line),
            ..container::Style::default().background(color)
        });
    button(
        row![
            text(game.name.as_str()).font(BOLD).size(14),
            space::horizontal(),
            stamp
        ]
        .height(Fill)
        .align_y(iced::Center),
    )
    .height(ROW_HEIGHT)
    .width(Fill)
    .padding([0, 12])
    .style(colors.button(selected))
    .on_press(Message::Open(Page::Game(game.app_id)))
    .into()
}

/// The rows at least partly visible when the list is scrolled `scroll`
/// pixels down a `viewport` that tall, with `total` rows of `row_height`.
pub fn visible_rows(scroll: f32, viewport: f32, row_height: f32, total: usize) -> Range<usize> {
    let first = (scroll.max(0.0) / row_height).floor() as usize;
    let end = ((scroll.max(0.0) + viewport) / row_height).ceil() as usize;
    first.min(total)..end.min(total)
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn at_the_top_the_first_rows_that_fit_are_drawn() {
        // Rows at 0–40, 40–80 and 80–120 px; the third is cut off at 100.
        assert_eq!(visible_rows(0.0, 100.0, 40.0, 1000), 0..3);
    }

    #[test]
    fn scrolled_down_the_rows_in_view_are_drawn() {
        // 410–510 px: row 10 (400–440) to row 12 (480–520).
        assert_eq!(visible_rows(410.0, 100.0, 40.0, 1000), 10..13);
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_short_list_draws_only_the_rows_it_has() {
        assert_eq!(visible_rows(0.0, 400.0, 40.0, 5), 0..5);
        // Scrolled further than a narrowed search reaches: nothing to draw.
        assert_eq!(visible_rows(4000.0, 400.0, 40.0, 5), 5..5);
    }
}

```rs
//! Two games side by side: verdict, what each asks of every part and how
//! this PC does, and the Linux facts (ROADMAP Phase 8).

use iced::widget::{Column, button, column, container, row, scrollable, text};
use iced::{Element, Fill};
use rigcheck_gamedb::Game;

use crate::game_page::{ROWS, linux_facts, requirement, result, row_id};
use crate::i18n::I18n;
use crate::library::{Status, stamp};
use crate::style::{BOLD, Colors};
use crate::{Message, Page};

/// One of the two games.
pub struct Side {
    pub app_id: u32,
    pub name: String,
    pub record: Option<Game>,
    pub status: Status,
}

pub fn view(a: Side, b: Side, i18n: &I18n, colors: Colors) -> Element<'static, Message> {
    let back = button(text(i18n.t("compare-back")).font(BOLD).size(13))
        .padding([7, 12])
        .style(colors.button(false))
        .on_press(Message::Open(Page::Game(b.app_id)));
    let label = |content: String| container(text(content).font(BOLD).size(13)).width(160);
    let cell = |content: Element<'static, Message>| container(content).width(Fill).padding([8, 10]);
    let line = |name: String, left: Element<'static, Message>, right: Element<'static, Message>| {
        row![label(name), cell(left), cell(right)].align_y(iced::Center)
    };
    let stamped = |side: &Side| -> Element<'static, Message> {
        let (text_label, color) = stamp(&side.status, i18n);
        container(text(text_label).font(BOLD).size(14))
            .padding([3, 8])
            .style(move |_| container::Style {
                text_color: Some(colors.line),
                ..container::Style::default().background(color)
            })
            .into()
    };

    let mut table = Column::new()
        .push(line(
            String::new(),
            text(a.name.clone()).font(BOLD).size(18).into(),
            text(b.name.clone()).font(BOLD).size(18).into(),
        ))
        .push(line(i18n.t("compare-verdict"), stamped(&a), stamped(&b)));
    for component in ROWS {
        let side = |side: &Side| -> Element<'static, Message> {
            let minimum = side.record.as_ref().and_then(|game| game.minimum.as_ref());
            column![
                text(requirement(minimum, component)).size(13),
                text(result(&side.status, component, i18n))
                    .font(BOLD)
                    .size(12),
            ]
            .spacing(2)
            .into()
        };
        table = table.push(line(i18n.t(row_id(component)), side(&a), side(&b)));
    }
    let facts = |side: &Side| side.record.as_ref().map(|game| linux_facts(game, i18n));
    if let (Some(left), Some(right)) = (facts(&a), facts(&b)) {
        for ((name, left), (_, right)) in left.into_iter().zip(right) {
            table = table.push(line(
                name,
                text(left).font(BOLD).size(13).into(),
                text(right).font(BOLD).size(13).into(),
            ));
        }
    }

    scrollable(
        column![
            back,
            text(i18n.t("compare-minimum-note")).color(colors.muted),
            container(table.spacing(4))
                .padding(10)
                .width(Fill)
                .style(move |_| colors.boxed(colors.panel)),
        ]
        .spacing(16)
        .padding([0, 6]),
    )
    .into()
}
